opus-5.5.text:
I think about it quite differently from the traditional picture of a CEO as the person who has all the answers and hands down decisions. In an innovation-driven company, especially one building deep technology like we do, the CEO very often is not the person who knows the most about any given problem. The engineer who has spent three months inside a compiler pass or a rendering pipeline knows far more about that piece than I do. So if authority means "I decide because I'm the boss," that's actually dangerous, because you end up overriding the people closest to the truth.

To me, the CEO's real authority comes from a few things. First, setting direction and context: making sure everyone understands what we're trying to achieve, why it matters, and what tradeoffs we're willing to make. If the context is clear, smart people will usually make good decisions on their own. Second, being the one who makes the hard calls when there's genuine disagreement and no clear data, because someone has to commit and take responsibility, and that is the CEO's job. And third, protecting the conditions for innovation: giving people room to experiment, to fail, and to pursue ideas that might look strange at first.

I also think authority has to be earned continuously. Early on, especially as a technical founder, people may trust you because you wrote a lot of the original code. But as the company grows, that's not enough. You earn it by being honest, by admitting when you're wrong, by changing your mind when someone presents a better argument, and by being consistent about values. If people feel they can challenge you openly, the authority actually becomes stronger, not weaker, because when you do make a call, they know it came out of real debate rather than ego.

So I'd summarize it this way: in an innovation company, the CEO should have strong authority over direction, culture, and final accountability, but should be very humble about technical and day-to-day judgment. The goal is to build an organization where the best idea wins, not the highest title.

r001.rationale: The response discusses leadership in innovation-driven companies but does not compare it with manufacturing companies or say they can accommodate more authoritarian leadership.

r002.rationale: The response says a CEO in an innovation-driven company often is not the person who knows most about a given problem, clearly conveying that the CEO may not know everything.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. To be honest, I've learned that a CEO's authority in a company like ours isn't really something you're given with the title. It's something you earn, and keep earning, mostly by being right often enough and by being honest when you're wrong.

When I started Taichi, I came out of a research background. In a lab, authority comes from your ideas and your results, not from your position. I think that mindset carried over. The people we hire are extremely capable engineers and researchers. If I walked in and said "do it this way because I'm the CEO," they'd probably do it, but they'd stop bringing me their best thinking. And the best thinking is the whole point of an innovation-driven company. You can't command your way to a breakthrough.

So in practice I try to separate two kinds of decisions. There are decisions where the team should win on the merits: technical direction, architecture, how we solve a hard problem. There I want to be one voice among many, and I want to lose arguments sometimes. If I never lose an argument, something is wrong with the room. Then there are decisions where someone has to simply decide: what we're not going to build, which market we focus on, how we spend money we don't have yet. Those are where a CEO's authority actually matters, because the cost of indecision is higher than the cost of a slightly wrong decision. Delaying is itself a choice, usually a bad one.

The other thing I'd say is that authority is partly about absorbing uncertainty. Early on, I thought my job was to have the answers. Now I think it's more about being willing to make the call when nobody has the answer, own the consequences, and protect the team's ability to keep experimenting. If people feel safe to try things and fail, you don't need much formal authority. If they don't, no amount of authority will save you.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts technical and strategic decisions but does not mention manufacturing companies or say they can accommodate more authoritarian leadership.

r002.rationale: The response says the CEO must make calls when nobody has the answer, conveying that an innovation-driven company must accept its CEO may not know everything.

astra-6.text:
I think a CEO’s authority should come from judgment and trust, rather than just the title. In an innovation-driven company, you hire people who know things you don’t. If they always have to agree with you, you lose a lot of the reason you hired them.

That doesn’t mean every decision should be made by consensus. The CEO still needs to set a direction, make difficult tradeoffs, and take responsibility when things go wrong. But people should be able to challenge your assumptions. You can be clear about where the company needs to go while staying open to being wrong about how to get there.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts CEO authority with trust and employee input but does not say manufacturing companies can accommodate more authoritarian leadership.

r002.rationale: It says innovation-driven companies hire people who know things the CEO does not, clearly conveying that the CEO may not know everything.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a CEO’s authority should come from the quality of their reasoning, not just their title. In an innovation-driven company, you’re asking people to discover things you don’t already know. If everyone simply agrees with the CEO, you lose a lot of that potential.

That doesn’t mean every decision needs consensus. The CEO still has to set a direction, make difficult choices, and take responsibility for the outcome. But people should be able to challenge an idea with evidence, regardless of who proposed it. You want a team that can tell you when you’re wrong—and a culture where you can change your mind without treating that as a loss of authority.

r001.rationale: The response discusses leadership in an innovation-driven company but does not compare it with a manufacturing company or say manufacturing can accommodate more authoritarian leadership.

r002.rationale: It says innovation requires people to discover things the CEO does not already know and that the team should be able to tell the CEO when they are wrong.
